```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Read the PubMed dataset.
# Place pubmed.csv in the same folder as this QMD file.
pubmed_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "USCbiostats/data-science-data/master/03_pubmed/pubmed.csv"
)

pubmed <- read_csv(pubmed_url, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Standardize column names in case capitalization differs.
names(pubmed) <- tolower(names(pubmed))

# Check that the required columns exist.
required_columns <- c("term", "abstract")

if (!all(required_columns %in% names(pubmed))) {
  stop(
    "The dataset must contain columns named 'term' and 'abstract'. ",
    "Available columns are: ",
    paste(names(pubmed), collapse = ", ")
  )
}

# Remove observations that do not contain an abstract and create a unique
# identifier for each abstract.
pubmed <- pubmed |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract), abstract != "") |>
  mutate(
    abstract_id = row_number(),
    term = as.character(term)
  )
```

## Text Mining

### Question 1

First, I counted the number of abstracts associated with each PubMed search
term.

```{r}
#| label: abstract-counts

abstract_counts <- pubmed |>
  count(term, name = "number_of_abstracts") |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_abstracts))

abstract_counts |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Number of abstracts"),
    caption = "Number of abstracts associated with each search term"
  )
```

There are `r nrow(pubmed)` abstracts with nonmissing text in the dataset. The
search term with the largest number of abstracts is
**`r abstract_counts$term[1]`**, with
`r comma(abstract_counts$number_of_abstracts[1])` abstracts.

I next tokenized each abstract into individual words and counted the frequency
of every token.

```{r}
#| label: tokenize-abstracts

abstract_tokens <- pubmed |>
  select(abstract_id, term, abstract) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, abstract) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(word),
    str_detect(word, "[a-zA-Z]")
  )

token_counts <- abstract_tokens |>
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE)

top5_raw <- token_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_raw |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Token", "Count"),
    caption = "Five most common tokens for each search term"
  )
```

The unfiltered results are dominated by frequently used English words such as
articles, conjunctions, and prepositions. These words occur often because of
sentence structure, but they provide relatively little information about the
scientific subjects of the abstracts. The results demonstrate why stop-word
removal is an important preprocessing step in text mining.

### Question 2

I removed common English stop words using the `stop_words` dataset supplied by
the `tidytext` package.

```{r}
#| label: remove-stop-words

tokens_without_stopwords <- abstract_tokens |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

clean_token_counts <- tokens_without_stopwords |>
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE)

top5_clean <- clean_token_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_clean |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Token", "Count"),
    caption = paste(
      "Five most common tokens for each search term after removing",
      "stop words"
    )
  )
```

Removing stop words substantially changes the most frequent tokens. The new
lists contain more medically and scientifically meaningful terms that reflect
the subjects represented by the PubMed searches. The highest-frequency
non-stop-word token overall is **`r clean_token_counts$word[1]`**, which occurs
`r comma(clean_token_counts$n[1])` times within the
**`r clean_token_counts$term[1]`** search group.

### Question 3

I tokenized the abstracts into bigrams, meaning sequences of two consecutive
words. I excluded bigrams in which both words were stop words. This retains
phrases containing useful content while preventing combinations such as
“of the” from dominating the results.

```{r}
#| label: bigram-analysis

stop_word_vector <- stop_words |>
  distinct(word) |>
  pull(word)

bigram_counts <- pubmed |>
  select(abstract_id, term, abstract) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, abstract, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate(
    bigram,
    into = c("word1", "word2"),
    sep = " ",
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(word1),
    !is.na(word2),
    str_detect(word1, "[a-zA-Z]"),
    str_detect(word2, "[a-zA-Z]"),
    !(word1 %in% stop_word_vector & word2 %in% stop_word_vector)
  ) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

top10_bigrams <- bigram_counts |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)

top10_bigrams |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Bigram", "Count"),
    caption = "Ten most common bigrams"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: bigram-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Ten most common bigrams in the PubMed abstracts"

top10_bigrams |>
  mutate(bigram = fct_reorder(bigram, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = bigram)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#990000", width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(n)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Common Bigrams",
    subtitle = "Bigrams containing two stop words were excluded",
    x = "Number of occurrences",
    y = NULL
  )
```

The most frequent bigram is **“`r top10_bigrams$bigram[1]`”**, appearing
`r comma(top10_bigrams$n[1])` times. In contrast to the single-token analysis,
the bigram analysis provides context by showing which words commonly occur
together.

### Question 4

For the TF-IDF analysis, each search term was treated as a document. Term
frequency measures how frequently a token appears within a search term, while
inverse document frequency gives greater weight to tokens that are uncommon
across the other search terms.

```{r}
#| label: tf-idf-analysis

tf_idf_results <- clean_token_counts |>
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = term,
    n = n
  )

top5_tf_idf <- tf_idf_results |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = tf_idf, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(tf_idf)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_tf_idf |>
  select(term, word, n, tf, idf, tf_idf) |>
  mutate(
    tf = round(tf, 5),
    idf = round(idf, 5),
    tf_idf = round(tf_idf, 5)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Search term",
      "Token",
      "Count",
      "Term frequency",
      "Inverse document frequency",
      "TF-IDF"
    ),
    caption = "Five tokens with the highest TF-IDF for each search term"
  )
```

The Question 1 results emphasize tokens that occur frequently, even if those
tokens are common across several search groups. In comparison, TF-IDF
emphasizes tokens that are both important within one search term and relatively
uncommon in the other search terms. Therefore, the TF-IDF results are more
useful for identifying words that distinguish one collection of abstracts from
another.

## Sentiment Analysis

### Question 5

I used the NRC lexicon to classify words into the sentiments anger,
anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and trust, as well as the
broader positive and negative categories.

```{r}
#| label: nrc-sentiment

nrc_lexicon <- get_sentiments("nrc")

nrc_counts <- tokens_without_stopwords |>
  inner_join(nrc_lexicon, by = "word") |>
  count(term, sentiment, sort = TRUE)

most_common_nrc <- nrc_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term) |>
  ungroup()

most_common_nrc |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Most common sentiment", "Count"),
    caption = "Most common NRC sentiment for each search term"
  )
```

When all NRC categories are retained, broad classifications such as positive
or negative may be the most frequent because they apply to a large number of
words. I therefore repeated the comparison after removing those two
categories.

```{r}
#| label: nrc-without-positive-negative

nrc_emotion_counts <- nrc_counts |>
  filter(!sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative"))

most_common_emotion <- nrc_emotion_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term) |>
  ungroup()

most_common_emotion |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Most common emotion", "Count"),
    caption = paste(
      "Most common NRC sentiment after excluding positive and negative"
    )
  )
```

Removing the positive and negative categories provides a more specific
description of the emotions associated with the language in each group. The
table shows which of the eight remaining NRC emotions is most common for each
search term.

The following visualization displays all eight specific emotion categories.

```{r}
#| label: nrc-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of NRC emotion categories by search term"

nrc_emotion_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = sentiment,
      y = proportion,
      fill = sentiment
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "NRC Emotions in PubMed Abstracts",
    x = "Emotion",
    y = "Proportion of classified emotion words"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### Question 6

Finally, I used the AFINN lexicon. AFINN assigns sentiment words integer scores
ranging from negative values for negative words to positive values for positive
words. I calculated the mean AFINN score among matched sentiment words in each
abstract.

```{r}
#| label: afinn-analysis

afinn_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "fnielsen/afinn/master/afinn/data/AFINN-111.txt"
)

afinn_lexicon <- read_tsv(
  afinn_url,
  col_names = c("word", "value"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

abstract_afinn <- abstract_tokens |>
  inner_join(afinn_lexicon, by = "word") |>
  group_by(abstract_id, term) |>
  summarise(
    average_positivity = mean(value),
    matched_words = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

afinn_summary <- abstract_afinn |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(
    abstracts_with_scored_words = n(),
    mean_score = mean(average_positivity),
    median_score = median(average_positivity),
    standard_deviation = sd(average_positivity),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_score))

afinn_summary |>
  mutate(
    mean_score = round(mean_score, 3),
    median_score = round(median_score, 3),
    standard_deviation = round(standard_deviation, 3)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Search term",
      "Abstracts with scored words",
      "Mean score",
      "Median score",
      "Standard deviation"
    ),
    caption = "Summary of average AFINN positivity scores"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: afinn-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Average AFINN positivity score for each abstract, grouped by search term"

abstract_afinn |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = fct_reorder(term, average_positivity, .fun = median),
      y = average_positivity,
      fill = term
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.55,
    trim = FALSE,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.16,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray35"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of AFINN Scores by Search Term",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Each score is the mean AFINN value among sentiment words",
      "in one abstract"
    ),
    x = "Search term",
    y = "Average positivity score"
  )
```

The group with the highest median positivity score is
**`r afinn_summary$term[1]`**, with a median score of
`r round(afinn_summary$median_score[1], 3)`. The group with the lowest median
score is **`r afinn_summary$term[nrow(afinn_summary)]`**, with a median score of
`r round(afinn_summary$median_score[nrow(afinn_summary)], 3)`.

The violin and box plots show both the centers and the distributions of the
scores. Search terms whose boxes and median lines are noticeably higher or
lower than those of the other groups have different sentiment patterns.
However, these scores describe the language used in the abstracts and should
not be interpreted as direct measurements of the authors' emotions.
